  "what_the_study_did": "This study investigated functional connectivity (FC) changes in the brains of human patients with thalamic pain and a macaque model of thalamic pain to identify cross-species convergence.",
  "what_it_found": "The study found convergent increases in functional connectivity between the amygdala and brainstem regions (specifically the basolateral amygdala and ventral tegmental area/midbrain) in both human patients and macaques with thalamic pain. Additionally, increased FC between the amygdala and the mediodorsal thalamus was observed in both species.",

    },
    {
      "quote": "This cross-species convergence provides new insights into the neurological mechanisms underlying thalamic pain, paving the way for further studies and the development of therapeutic strategies.",
      "topic": "Implications for therapy"
    },
    {
      "quote": "In humans, the FC between the amygdala on the nonaffected side and the brainstem, specifically between the BLA and VTA, significantly increased in the thalamic pain condition.",
      "topic": "Human findings"
    },

      "quote": "A macaque model of thalamic pain mirrored these results with increased FC between the amygdala on the nonaffected side and brainstem, and more specifically between the BLA and midbrain.",
      "topic": "Macaque findings"
    },
    {
      "quote": "Conversely, a significant pain-related increase in FC between the amygdala and MD, which was the most prominent FC change observed in the macaque model of thalamic pain (Fig 7), was also reproduced in human patients.",
      "topic": "MD and amygdala FC"
    },
    {
      "quote": "The present study showing the cross-species convergence of the pain-related FC changes advances our understanding of the causality of thalamic pain in human patients using a macaque model.",

    }
